claims.text: Toughness retention in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys is governed by dynamic strain aging.
Moderate strain rates promote an optimal level of dislocation mobility in CrMnFeCoNi.
The dislocation mobility produced at moderate strain rates increases energy dissipation and toughness.
Very high strain rates cause dislocation locking in CrMnFeCoNi.
Dislocation locking at very high strain rates causes a transition to brittle failure.
The as-cast and thermomechanically processed CrMnFeCoNi states have homogeneous microstructures.
Strain rate will be varied from approximately 10^-4 s^-1 to 10^2 s^-1 during tensile testing.
Dislocation structures and dynamic-strain-aging signatures can be tracked using in-situ straining/TEM and post-mortem TEM.
Serrated flow and dislocation-cell formation are signatures of dynamic strain aging in this system.
At moderate strain rates, solute atoms assist dislocation mobility through dynamic strain aging.
Solute-assisted dislocation mobility permits greater energy absorption and enhances toughness retention.
At very high strain rates, dynamic strain aging instead locks dislocations and causes premature fracture and toughness loss.
Relative to the intermediate-rate baseline, moderately higher strain rates will increase toughness and produce serrated flow and mobile dislocation patterns.
Very high strain rates will produce pronounced flow serrations, locked dislocation networks, and lower ductility and toughness.
The predicted behavior is restricted to CrMnFeCoNi tested at room temperature after identical pre-deformation conditions.
Changes in composition or thermal history may produce different strain-rate responses.
The beneficial and detrimental dynamic-strain-aging regimes are predicted to generate a non-monotonic relationship between strain rate and toughness.

contradictions.description: The material is said to include both as-cast and thermomechanically processed states, which entail different processing histories, while the conditions and boundary describe specimens as having identical pre-deformation conditions. Identical final heat treatment does not by itself make these initial processing states identical.
